How I Use AI for Documentation Operations

A practical walkthrough of using AI-assisted workflows for code-level analysis, documentation auditing, and release communication at enterprise scale.

Over the past year, I have been using AI-assisted workflows (primarily through Cursor and LLM-based code analysis) as a core part of my documentation operations. This is not about generating content with a prompt. It is about using AI as a research and analysis partner to make documentation work faster, more accurate, and more scalable.

Here are the patterns that have worked well.

1. Codebase-to-Documentation Auditing

One of the hardest problems in technical writing is keeping documentation accurate as the product evolves. Features change, UI elements move, operators get added, and the documentation silently falls behind.

I use AI to compare what the documentation says against what the codebase actually implements. For example, I audited condition builder documentation by having AI navigate the Angular/TypeScript source to enumerate all supported comparison operators, then compared that list against what the docs covered. The result: three entire operator categories were missing from the documentation, and several operator descriptions were mislabeled.

Without AI, this audit would have required manually reading through component source files, service definitions, and enum declarations. With AI, it took under an hour.

2. Root Cause Investigation

When a team member reported that changelog headings in the marketplace connector details page were not rendering correctly, I used AI to trace the issue through the component tree: from the Angular template that renders the changelog markdown, to the SCSS styles that control heading appearance.

AI identified that the .notes-container h2 CSS rule was forcing version headings to render as small grey text (1rem, #9c9c9c), while h3 headings ("Bug Fixes") had no explicit styling and inherited larger default sizes. The visual hierarchy was inverted.

This kind of cross-file investigation (template → component → stylesheet) is exactly where AI excels: it can hold the full context of multiple files simultaneously and trace data flow faster than manual navigation.

3. Metadata Quality Analysis at Scale

When the product's Content Library showed duplicate categories in its filter panel, I used AI to investigate how category metadata flows from individual connector repositories through the SDK to the marketplace UI. This involved:

  • Finding the canonical category list in the SDK source code
  • Identifying the keywords field in connector.yaml as the source of truth per connector
  • Enumerating which connectors used non-canonical category names
  • Building a mapping of old names to canonical names
  • Generating bulk remediation scripts

The entire investigation, from "why are there duplicate categories" to "here is the fix and the list of affected repositories," was completed in a single working session.

4. Release Communication Quality

When drafting release notes from JIRA tickets, AI helps translate engineering-focused ticket descriptions into customer-facing language. The key is not asking AI to write the release notes from scratch, but to:

  • Extract the customer-visible behavior change from the ticket
  • Remove backend implementation details (database projections, class annotations, and so on)
  • Verify affected version accuracy
  • Group fixes by product area for readability

This produces release notes that answer "what changed for me" instead of "what the engineer fixed," which is consistently more useful for customers.

5. Stakeholder Communication Drafting

A less obvious but equally valuable use: AI helps draft clear, non-technical summaries of technical findings for managers and cross-functional stakeholders. When I need to explain a complex metadata quality problem to someone who understands the PR process but not the SDK internals, AI helps me find the right level of detail.

What Does Not Work

A few patterns I have learned to avoid:

  • Generating documentation content from scratch: AI-generated content without source verification tends to be plausible but inaccurate. I use AI for research and analysis, not for authoring final content
  • Trusting AI conclusions without verification: AI can confidently report incorrect findings. Every AI-assisted investigation needs a human verification step before acting on the results
  • Over-automating stakeholder communication: AI drafts need human judgment on tone, context, and what to include or omit. The draft is a starting point, not the final message

The Takeaway

AI does not replace documentation expertise. What it does is extend the reach of a documentation team, especially a small one. It turns "I would need engineering help to verify this" into "I can check this against the codebase myself." It turns "auditing 400 connectors would take weeks" into "I can enumerate the issues in an afternoon."

For documentation professionals working in enterprise software, AI-assisted code analysis is the highest-leverage skill to develop right now. It does not require becoming a developer. It requires knowing what questions to ask and how to verify the answers.
